title.narrative: Quality Urban Development and Sustainable Interventions for Jerusalem’s Old City (QUDSI)

description.narrative:
Jerusalem has always been at the center of Palestinians trade, transport, tourism, and culture, as well as diplomacy, although it has yet to serve as the capital city of modern-day State of Palestine as envisioned by the Palestinians. Most countries and leading cities of the world, especially those that are major destinations, have a thriving tourism sector. Compared to other destination cities, East Jerusalem unfortunately has much to be desired in this regard. Related to this, there are no major community initiatives tailored to not only the needs of the local Palestinian community within Jerusalem’s Old City, but to humanity more broadly through tourists either living, working or visiting Jerusalem, as well as hosting and engaging foreigners – whether they are independent travelers, religious pilgrims, resident expatriates, or visiting professionals and students.
Tourism is a catalyst for the local economy and a cross-cutting element incorporating various economic sectors, and it is expected reciprocally, that tourist and community centers support the development of cities, its visitors, residents and business communities and definitely its rich culture and heritage. These centers provide each beneficiary with a valuable offering, which enhances the development of tourism-mindedness, intellectual vigor, social friendships, and business relationships. As such tourism is a people-based economic activity built on social interaction. By opening the doors to employment opportunities and decent livelihood, leading skills and capacity development, tourism can have a strong transformative impact on communities.
Similarly, tourism-based initiatives promote understanding, the spread of information and contact development through networking. They also provide inclusive and enjoyable venues for rest, leisure, stimulating activities, entertaining international links, and useful services. Tourists and tourism represent a core element of Jerusalem’s Old City, and specifically new projects economic development strategy. With tourism representing an opportunity to constantly revitalize and diversify experiences, promote local economic development, involve many different professional sectors, and bring new uses to the tourism sector a unique cooperation between UN-Habitat and the European Union (EU) was created.
The QUDSI Project is initiated to fundamentally increase tourism-centered opportunities via Hub-based comprehensive interventions to serve and upgrade tourism through its living stones; by advancing and upgrading professional development for Jerusalemites in general and those serving the Old City of Jerusalem in specific. Through the foreseen support of the European Union and local donors , UN-Habitat have Created a plan to revive a very pressing trilateral track that will overall feed the tourism’s sector’s professional capacity building, the three main components are the Youth, Technological Empowerment and Innovation and last but not least Economic Empowerment.
With the absence of official Palestinian existence and rule in East Jerusalem, increasing community-based interventions are taking a role towards Palestinian steadfastness and empowerment in East Jerusalem. Numerous professional and well-connected sectorial based entities are executing small to large scale interventions towards up-lifting living standards and quality of work and life of the local Palestinian community. Major sectors such as housing, rehabilitation, economy, tourism, education, youth, and culture are placing technical and financial efforts towards the East Jerusalem’s well-being and development.
Unfortunately, if any, there is minimal inner-sectorial and inner-governmental coordination between the different key players to document, organize and share of data to complement each other’s work and minimize if not eliminate duplication of work and effort. Even less coordination exist at the cross-sectorial level; where most sectors and most governmental entities focus on inner boundaries of their work without coordination their efforts towards cross-cutting platforms and more importantly to share complementary tools and techniques to insure proper coordination that will harvest the benefits for the general implementation and functioning of their interventions.
